name: Tarok
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Sibomana, Leo. 1980. Grundzüge der Phonologie des Tarok (Yergam). Afrika und Übersee 63; also Longtau, Selbut R. 2008. Tarok language: Its Basic Principles and Grammar. (neither online)
earlier_scan.note: Dedicated phonology + full grammar exist offline; Blench Tarokoid PDF (read via Wayback) has no stress statement

sources.citation: StressTyp2 (2015 SQL archive, local copy) and PHOIBLE (UPSID 631, AA 826) entries for Tarok
sources.note: Tarok appears in StressTyp2 only in the ISO-639 code table ('yer','NG','L','Tarok'); no stress entry. PHOIBLE has segment inventories only.

sources.citation: Onah, Patrick El-kanemi & Israel T. Gampyal. 2022. A phonological description of Tarok. Journal of English and Communication in Africa 5(3&4): 1-23.
sources.note: p.18 'Suprasegmental Phonology of Tarok' lists 'syllables, stress, tone and intonation' as suprasegmentals, but only a syllable section (p.18, following Longtau 2008) and a 'Tone and Intonation' section (p.19: 'Like most Nigerian languages, Tarok is tonal. There are three level or static tones (high, mid and low) and two kinetic or gliding tones') follow; the conclusion (p.21) claims stress was described but no stress statement exists in the paper.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2020. Research on the Plateau languages of Central Nigeria. Afrika und Übersee 93: 3-44. DOI 10.15460/auue.2021.93.1.209
sources.note: Survey of Plateau research; §2.1 Tarokoid notes Tarok has 'a series of papers on grammar and morphology and a substantial draft dictionary (Longtau 2008; Blench & Longtau 2011)'; no stress or tone statement for Tarok.

sources.citation: Longtau, Selbut R. 2008 [2022 edited electronic edition]. The Tarok Language: Its Basic Principles and Grammar Sketch. Jos: Development Alternatives, Research & Training (DART). Print ed. xiv+241 pp.
sources.note: Chapter 2 'Sound System' (2.3 Syllable patterns, print p.21; 2.4 Word patterns p.25; 2.6 Tonemes p.34) treats the syllable as a tone-carrying unit ('Each syllable carries one and only one tone'), describes three level and two contour tones with high lexical and grammatical functional load; the word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the full text (only 'distress'), nor 'accent'/'prominence' in a prosodic sense. Silent on stress.

sources.citation: Robinson, J. O. S. 1976. His and hers morphology: the strange case of the Tarok possessives. In Hyman, Jacobson & Schuh (eds.), Papers in African linguistics in honour of William E. Welmers (SAL Supplement 6), 201-209. Los Angeles: UCLA.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: WALS's only Tarok source; morphology of possessive reduplication, which interacts with tone. Unlikely to state stress but cheap to check if SAL supplements come online.

sources.citation: Longtau, Selbut R. 1993. A formal Tarok phonology. Afrika und Übersee 76: 15-40.

sources.note: Second dedicated phonology; likely a formal syllable/tone treatment. Longtau 2008 says it is folded into the grammar's chapter 2, which has no stress statement, so expected to be silent too, but it should be checked.
